planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Wasabi is a vigorous, sun-tolerant coleus cultivar with bright chartreuse-green, deeply ruffled and jagged-edged leaves, providing bold color contrast in both sun and shade plantings.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Wasabi is a widely grown, vigorous coleus cultivar bred for improved sun tolerance, distinguished by large, brilliantly chartreuse-green leaves with deeply cut, ruffled, almost oak-leaf-like edges. Its intensely bright, almost glowing chartreuse color makes it an outstanding accent against darker-foliaged companions in both container plantings and garden beds, and the bold, ruffled leaf texture adds visual interest beyond color alone. Like other modern sun coleus, Wasabi handles considerably more direct sun than older shade-only coleus varieties, though the color is often most vivid with some afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear, since coleus flowers are insignificant and pinching redirects the plant's energy into larger, more colorful foliage and a fuller, more branched habit. In zone 9's long warm season, Wasabi can grow into a large, impressive specimen by late summer.

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely cut, lacy, copper-orange leaves edged in chartreuse-green, an unusual warm color combination well suited to hanging baskets and container edges.

directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely dissected, lacy-textured leaves in a warm copper-orange center fading to a chartreuse-green edge, an unusual combination that reads as warm and glowing rather than the cooler purples and reds common among coleus. Its cascading, trailing habit makes it especially well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of large containers, where it spills gracefully over the rim, and the fine, ferny leaf texture provides contrast against bolder, broad-leaved companion plants. Like most coleus, it performs best with some protection from the most intense midday sun in zone 9, coloring up most vividly with morning sun and afternoon shade. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage denser, bushier trailing growth.

common_name: Fishnet Stockings Coleus (Netted Chartreuse-and-Green Veined Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Fishnet Stockings is a coleus cultivar with bright chartreuse leaves overlaid by a fine, dark green net-like vein pattern, giving the foliage a distinctive lace or netted texture unlike solid-colored coleus varieties.

directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Fishnet Stockings is a distinctively patterned coleus cultivar whose bright chartreuse-green leaves are overlaid with a fine, dark green network of veins, giving the foliage a netted or lace-like texture that reads as a pattern rather than a solid color from a distance. This intricate veining makes it a striking textural accent in mixed containers and shaded beds, standing out clearly next to solid-colored or broadly variegated coleus companions. Like most coleus, it prefers some protection from the harshest midday sun in zone 9, developing its clearest patterning with morning sun and afternoon shade. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy focused on foliage production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a fuller, more compact, well-branched habit.

common_name: Alabama Sunset Coleus (Classic Orange-Red Heirloom Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Alabama Sunset is a classic heirloom coleus cultivar with warm orange-red leaves veined in maroon and edged in chartreuse, a longtime favorite sun-tolerant selection for bold summer foliage color.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Alabama Sunset is a classic, long-popular coleus cultivar bearing warm orange-red leaves marked with darker maroon veining and a bright chartreuse-green edge, a fiery, autumnal color combination that has kept it a garden favorite for decades. It tolerates considerably more direct sun than traditional shade coleus, making it a versatile choice for both sunny mixed borders and shadier spots, though the richest, most saturated coloring develops with some protection from the most intense afternoon sun in zone 9. The vigorous, upright, well-branched plants provide season-long color without relying on flowers, which should be pinched off as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage. Pinch growing tips periodically through the season to maintain a dense, bushy habit and prevent the plant from becoming leggy.

common_name: Black Dragon Coleus (Deep Maroon-Black Ruffled Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Black Dragon is a coleus cultivar with deeply ruffled, near-black maroon leaves edged in a thin band of bright magenta-red, providing dramatic dark foliage contrast in mixed plantings.

directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Black Dragon is a dramatic coleus cultivar with deeply cut, ruffled, near-black maroon leaves edged in a narrow band of bright magenta-red, providing some of the darkest foliage color available in coleus and a strong textural accent from the heavily serrated leaf margins. Its near-black coloring makes it an outstanding foil for chartreuse, silver, or brightly colored companion plants in mixed containers and borders, where the contrast draws the eye immediately. Like most coleus, it develops its darkest, richest color with some protection from the most intense midday sun in zone 9, though it tolerates more light than old-fashioned shade-only coleus varieties. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a full, dense, well-branched habit.
